script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education Examination 2026. English Language Paper 3. Listening and Integrated Skills. Digital Literacy for All - High Stamina Mock Exam. This recording will be played once only.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: The entire broadcast will last approximately one hour and fifteen minutes. Part A. Task 1. You are a student volunteer helping at the Kowloon Bay Community Hall. You will hear a phone conversation between a fellow volunteer, Justin Cheng, and a local resident, Mrs. Wong Sau Lan. Complete the registration form. You now have two minutes to study the task. (120-second pause)

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: Good morning! This is Justin from the 'Digital Literacy for All' volunteer team. I'm calling from our new Kowloon Bay regional office. We've just received your inquiry through the community center website. Am I speaking with Mrs. Wong?

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: Oh, hello... yes, this is Mrs. Wong. Sorry, I was just... I was just staring at this tablet my daughter bought me for my birthday. It's sitting here like a very expensive paperweight. I'm almost afraid to touch it! Every time I look at it, a new notification pops up and I'm sure I've been hacked already. Is this the help program I heard about on David Lam's radio show?

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: Haha, don't worry, Mrs. Wong! You're definitely not alone. Many of our residents feel the same way. And yes, this is the official program sponsored by the Innovation and Technology Bureau. My job today is to get you registered for our upcoming workshop series so we can turn that paperweight back into a useful tool. First, I just need to confirm some details. Your full name is Wong Sau Lan, is that correct?

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: That's right. Wong is W-O-N-G, and Sau Lan is S-A-U, then L-A-N. My grandson tells me I should have a 'cool' English name like 'Tiffany' or 'Crystal', but I've been Sau Lan for sixty-eight years and I think I'll stick with it!

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: Wong Sau Lan. Got it. And I have your age down here as sixty-eight. That's a great age to start—my own grandmother is seventy-two and she's just started using social media to find old school friends! Now, I have your contact number from our caller ID as 9123 4567. Is that the best number to reach you on?

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: Yes, that's my mobile. It's an old one, but it works. And for my address, I'm over in Fortune Estate. It's quite a large estate, so you'll need the block number—I'm in Block 4, on the twelfth floor. It's very convenient because it's right next to the shopping center.

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: Block 4, Fortune Estate. Noted. Now, Mrs. Wong, how would you describe your current tech experience? Are you comfortable with basic things like sending a text message, or are we starting from the very beginning?

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: Oh, I'm an absolute beginner, Justin. A total novice. I can answer the phone if it rings, but that's about it. If I have to type anything or find a specific 'app'—that's the word, right?—I get very flustered. My biggest fear is the scams. I read in the Sing Tao Daily about seniors losing their whole life savings just by clicking a link in an SMS. It makes me want to throw the whole phone in the bin!

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: I completely understand. Cybersecurity is actually our most popular module. We'll show you exactly how to spot those fake messages so you can feel safe. Aside from security, what's the one thing you really want to be able to do once you've finished the course?

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: The photos, Justin. My daughter lives in Vancouver, and she's always sending me photos of my grandson, Leo. He's growing up so fast! She says she sends them on 'WhatsApp', but I can never find them, or the screen goes dark before I can see them properly. I want to be able to have a video call where I can actually see him talking to me. It would mean the world to me.

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: Video calls and photo sharing. We can definitely make that happen. It's much easier than you think once you know where to click. Now, what kind of device are you using? You mentioned a tablet earlier?

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: I have the tablet, which is an iPad, but for my daily use, I have an old iPhone 8. My son gave it to me when he upgraded. It's a bit small, and the battery doesn't last very long, but I like that it has a physical button at the bottom. The new ones without buttons look very confusing!

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: The iPhone 8 is a classic! It's perfect for learning the basics. Now, for our workshops, we have a few centers. Since you're in Fortune Estate, the Kowloon Bay Community Hall is definitely the closest for you. It's only a five-minute walk from the MTR. We have a new session starting on Monday mornings from 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM. Does that work for you?

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: Monday morning is perfect. I usually go to the market early, so I can come straight to the hall after that. Oh, and Justin, I have one more request. My eyesight isn't what it used to be. Do you have those instruction books with the very large font? I struggle with the tiny manuals that come with the phones.

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: Yes, we have specifically designed 'Senior-Friendly' guidebooks with extra-large font and very clear diagrams. I'll make sure a copy is reserved for you. And because you are over sixty-five, the registration fee is completely waived. It's part of the government subsidy. You don't have to pay a single cent.

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: Free of charge? That's wonderful. I heard about the program on the radio this morning—I think it was the show with David Lam? He sounded very enthusiastic about it.

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: That's the one! Beatrice Thorne was on his show earlier. Well, Mrs. Wong, you're all set. You'll receive a confirmation letter in the mail by Friday. We look forward to seeing you at the Kowloon Bay Community Hall next Monday!

script.speaker: Mrs Wong
script.text: Thank you, Justin. You've been very patient with an old lady. I'm actually a little bit excited now!

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: That's the spirit! See you soon, Mrs. Wong.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: (60-second pause to tidy up answers)

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: Task 2. You will hear a keynote presentation by Beatrice Thorne, Lead Coordinator of the 'Digital Literacy for All' program. Listen to the presentation and complete the notes. You now have two minutes to study the task. (120-second pause)

script.speaker: Beatrice Thorne
script.text: Good morning, everyone. It is an honor to be here at the 2026 Digital Inclusion Summit. Today, I want to talk about a phenomenon that is often discussed in economic terms, but rarely in human terms. I'm talking about the 'Silver Tsunami'. In just a few years, more than a third of Hong Kong's population will be over the age of sixty-five. We are one of the fastest-aging cities in the world. But while we focus on healthcare and housing for our seniors, we are ignoring a silent crisis: digital exclusion. Imagine a world where you cannot buy a bus ticket, book a doctor's appointment, or even pay for your groceries because you don't understand the interface on a glass screen. For many of our seniors, the 'Smart City' feels like a 'Locked City'.

script.speaker: Beatrice Thorne
script.text: Let's look at the data. Our most recent survey from late 2025 shows that while smartphone ownership among seniors has risen, the actual adoption rate for daily essential technology—meaning things beyond just making a phone call—is still only around 35%. That means 65% of our elderly population are effectively 'digitally blind' to the services they need most. Why is this? Through our focus groups, we've identified two primary barriers. The first is physical: visual impairment. Standard app designs use tiny fonts and low-contrast colors that are impossible for aging eyes to navigate. The second barrier is structural: complex interfaces. We design apps for 'digital natives' who understand the logic of swipes and hidden menus. For a senior, these interfaces aren't intuitive; they are obstacles.

script.speaker: Beatrice Thorne
script.text: To combat this, the Innovation and Technology Bureau has officially launched our flagship initiative: the Digital Hubs. Our goal is to establish fifty of these hubs across all eighteen districts of Hong Kong. These aren't just classrooms; they are community spaces where tech meets empathy. And I'm proud to announce that we have secured a total approved budget of $400 Million HKD to fund this rollout over the next three years. This isn't just a pilot project; it's a permanent shift in our social infrastructure. Our curriculum is divided into three distinct modules. Module 1, 'Device Basics', focuses on the physical handling of technology—charging, gestures, and settings. Module 2, 'Secure Surfing', is our most critical. It teaches seniors how to identify phishing, manage passwords, and protect their privacy. Finally, Module 3, 'e-Government Services', shows them how to use the 'iAM Smart' app and other digital platforms to access their health records and social benefits.

script.speaker: Beatrice Thorne
script.text: But how will we know if we are succeeding? We aren't just counting the number of people who walk through our doors. We are tracking two primary success metrics. First, we are looking at total app downloads for essential government services within our target demographics. Second, and perhaps more importantly, we are monitoring satisfaction rates through our dedicated Digital Literacy Hotline. If our seniors are calling us with confidence rather than confusion, we know we are on the right track. Our next major strategic review is scheduled for March 15, 2026. By then, we hope to have thirty of the fifty hubs fully operational. Our core philosophy is 'Inclusion for All'. We are building a city where technology is a bridge, not a wall. Our motto is simple, but powerful: 'No one left behind'. Whether you are eight or eighty, the digital world belongs to you. Thank you.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: (60-second pause to tidy up answers)

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: Task 3. David Lam is interviewing Dr. Samuel Ng on the show 'City Pulse'. Listen to the interview and complete the information sheet. You now have two minutes to study the task. (120-second pause)

script.speaker: David Lam
script.text: Welcome back to 'City Pulse'. We're continuing our deep dive into digital literacy. While Beatrice Thorne's hubs are teaching the basics, there's a darker side to the digital world that even tech-savvy people are struggling with. I'm talking about AI-driven fraud. Joining us today is Dr. Samuel Ng, an AI Ethics Consultant who advises the government on emerging tech risks. Welcome, Samuel.

script.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ng
script.text: Thanks, David. It's a pleasure to be here, though I wish I were here to talk about more pleasant topics! The reality is that the tools we use to create amazing art and videos are also being weaponized by criminals.

script.speaker: David Lam
script.text: You're referring to 'Deepfakes'. For our listeners who might have heard the term but aren't sure what it means, can you give us a simple definition?

script.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ng
script.text: Certainly. A Deepfake is essentially AI-generated fake media. It uses powerful 'deep learning' algorithms to replace the face or voice of one person with another. It can create a video of someone saying things they never said, or a voice recording that sounds exactly like a loved one. And this is the primary risk to our seniors: Family Impersonation. We're seeing a rise in 'Grandparent Scams' where a criminal calls a senior, sounding exactly like their grandson in trouble, asking for an urgent bank transfer. It's incredibly effective because it bypasses our logical defenses through emotional manipulation.

script.speaker: David Lam
script.text: That's terrifying. How can a normal person possibly tell the difference if the voice sounds identical?

script.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ng
script.text: It's getting harder, but there are still 'tells'. In videos, look for unnatural blinking patterns—AI often struggles to simulate the random frequency of human blinks. Also, look at the edges of the face for slight blurring. In audio calls, listen for robotic glitches or unnatural pauses. AI voices often have a strange, metallic quality in the higher frequencies. But my top recommendation isn't technical; it's the 'Safe Word' system. Every family should have a secret word or phrase that they use only in emergencies. If the person on the phone can't provide the safe word, it's a scam. Hang up immediately.

script.speaker: David Lam
script.text: A 'Safe Word'. That's a great, low-tech solution to a high-tech problem. Now, what about our official government security? We have the 'iAM Smart' app, but I hear the adoption of two-factor authentication, or 2FA, is still quite low.

script.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ng
script.text: It is. Our data shows that only 25% of active mobile users in Hong Kong have enabled 2FA on all their critical accounts. That's dangerously low. Most people find the extra step of a code or a fingerprint scan to be 'annoying', but that one extra step is what stops 90% of account takeovers. I've proposed to the Education Bureau that we should have mandatory cybersecurity training in all secondary schools. We need our students to be the 'tech guardians' for their parents and grandparents. Looking ahead, the future of security is in Biometrics—using our unique biological signatures, like iris scans or vein patterns, to prove who we are. But even that comes with an associated privacy risk: data breaches. If your password is stolen, you can change it. If your iris scan is stolen, you're in real trouble. That's why the Cyber Security Office is working on new encryption standards. If anyone listening has been a victim of a scam, or needs technical help with their security settings, they should contact the Cyber Security Office immediately.

script.speaker: David Lam
script.text: Thank you, Dr. Ng. That's a lot for our listeners to think about. Stay safe out there, everyone.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: (60-second pause to tidy up answers)

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: Task 4. Beatrice Thorne, Cecilia Ma, and Justin Cheng are finalizing the plans for the 'Digital Literacy Carnival 2026'. Listen to their meeting and complete the matrix. You now have two minutes to study the task. (120-second pause)

script.speaker: Beatrice Thorne
script.text: Alright team, let's bring this home. We are just two months away from our biggest event yet: the Digital Literacy Carnival 2026. We've finally locked in the dates with the Leisure and Cultural Services Department. It will be a three-day event from January 12th to the 14th, 2026. We've secured Victoria Park as the venue—specifically soccer pitches 3 and 4. It's the most accessible location in the city.

script.speaker: Cecilia Ma
script.text: That's great news, Beatrice. Based on our social media engagement, I'm projecting an expected attendee count of at least 15,000 people over the weekend. We need to make sure the flow is managed. Our main attraction will be the 'Live VR Demo' on the center stage. We'll be showing seniors how they can 'travel' to Paris or London using virtual reality headsets. It's going to be a huge crowd-puller.

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: I've already started a list of immediate actions. First, I need to book the security staff. With 15,000 people, we need at least twenty guards on-site at all times. Second, I'm working with the branding agency to design the orange vests for our volunteers. We want them to be highly visible. The logo imagery we've chosen is a 'Hand holding a stylized Smartphone'—it symbolizes the human connection to technology. And of course, we'll have our official motto 'Patience First' printed in large white letters across the front.

script.speaker: Cecilia Ma
script.text: I love the logo, Justin. Regarding the logistics, I've set a hard vendor bid deadline for November 30th. We need to have all our booth contractors signed by then. I've also allocated $5 Million HKD specifically for the marketing budget. We're going to use a mix of bus body ads, radio spots, and social media influencers who have a senior following.

script.speaker: Beatrice Thorne
script.text: Five million should be sufficient. My two critical priorities for the final push are: first, senior-friendly signage. Every sign in Victoria Park needs to be high-contrast with at least a 72-point font size. We can't have people getting lost at a literacy carnival! Second, the student volunteer training. Justin, I'm putting you in charge of that. I want every volunteer to undergo a four-hour empathy workshop. They need to understand that their job isn't just to fix the tech; it's to fix the fear.

script.speaker: Justin
script.text: Consider it done, Beatrice. 'Patience First' will be our guiding light.

script.speaker: Beatrice Thorne
script.text: Excellent. Let's make this the most inclusive event in Hong Kong's history. Meeting adjourned.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: (60-second pause to tidy up answers) This is the end of Part A. Now, turn to Part B.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: Part B. Introduction. You are Chris Wong, an assistant to Cecilia Ma. You will hear a briefing session Cecilia gives to the senior volunteers for the MTR Help Desk program. As you listen, take notes which may help you to complete the tasks in the question-answer book. You will have five minutes to study the Part B Information Directory and the tasks. (Pause 5m)

script.speaker: Cecilia Ma
script.text: Good morning, everyone. Welcome to our frontline team. As Chris here will tell you, we've been working around the clock to get the MTR Help Desks ready for our 2026 launch. You are the heart of this program. When a citizen is frustrated, you are the one who provides the 'Patience First' experience. First, let's talk about our locations. We've finalized our three main hubs. Mong Kok Station is our busiest, and we'll be located right near Exit D2. Central Station will have a desk in the Pedder Street concourse. And for our commuters from the New Territories, we have a station in Kowloon Tong, right at the East Rail Line interchange. These are high-traffic areas, so expect to be busy!

script.speaker: Cecilia Ma
script.text: I want to be very clear about our hierarchy of tasks. We've divided them into three levels: Bronze, Silver, and Gold. Bronze tasks are the foundation—adjusting phone settings like font size or brightness, and connecting to public Wi-Fi. Silver tasks are about social connection—messaging, sharing photos, and making video calls. And Gold tasks are the most sensitive. These involve e-Banking, using the 'iAM Smart' app, and overall cybersecurity. As a general rule, if you are helping with a Gold task, you MUST have a second volunteer present to witness the interaction. We need to protect both the citizen and ourselves.

script.speaker: Cecilia Ma
script.text: Regarding the budget, there's been some confusion in the press. Let me set the record straight for your notes, Chris. The total budget approved by the Innovation Bureau is $400 Million HKD. Please ignore any earlier reports from 2023 that mentioned $200 Million—that was an early proposal that was significantly increased to meet our current scale. Of this $400 Million, we have specifically earmarked $50 Million for the 'Volunteer Support Fund'. This is to cover your travel expenses, your meals, and your uniforms. We don't want your generosity to be a financial burden on you.

script.speaker: Cecilia Ma
script.text: Now, for the 'Red Phone' protocol. This is critical. If you suspect a citizen is currently being targeted by a scam—for example, if they've received a suspicious message asking for an immediate transfer—do NOT attempt to investigate it yourself. Every desk has a dedicated 'Red Phone' line. Pick it up and it connects directly to the Police Anti-Deception Coordination Centre at 18222. Your role is to provide emotional support while the professionals handle the case. And Chris, please ensure the 'Citizen Interaction Logs' for these cases are marked as 'S-Tier'. We need to track these incidents separately for our quarterly report to the Finance Committee.

script.speaker: Cecilia Ma
script.text: Lastly, a word on the 2023 Archive document that was accidentally included in some of the older volunteer folders. It mentions Sha Tin Station as a launch location and a budget of $200 million. PLEASE DISREGARD THIS ENTIRELY. Sha Tin was cancelled due to the major renovations there, and as I said, the budget has doubled. We are operating on the 2026 plan only. Our focus is on the MTR stations I mentioned earlier: Mong Kok, Central, and Kowloon Tong. Chris, make sure you emphasize this in the follow-up email to all mentors. We can't have people showing up to the wrong station in January! Alright, let's get into the details of the 'Patience First' campaign...

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: This is the end of the Integrated Skills recording. You now have 1 hour and 15 minutes to complete your tasks. (End of simulation)

To: Cecilia Ma
Subject: Feedback on Help Desk Layout

Hi Cecilia, we've reviewed the proposed layout for the Mong Kok D2 desk. We are concerned about the width of the desk—it shouldn't exceed 2 meters to avoid blocking the passenger flow near the 'Community Zone'. Also, regarding the Kowloon Tong location, please ensure all cabling is tucked under the flooring for safety. We recommend using wireless tablets to minimize trip hazards.

data_file.title: The Digital Divide in 2026: A Growing Gap?
data_file.content: Despite government efforts, 25% of seniors still feel isolated from digital services. 'It's not just the hardware,' says urban sociologist Dr. Aris Thorne. 'It's the fear of being exploited by tech that's designed for speed, not empathy.' The upcoming 'Digital Literacy for All' program is seen as a critical life-raft for those left behind by the 2030 smart city transition.
